Ancient Indian history

Mauryan empire: rulers, administration and sources

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

The Mauryan empire (about 321 to 185 BCE) was founded by Chandragupta Maurya, who overthrew the Nandas of Magadha. Under Bindusara and Ashoka it covered most of the subcontinent, ruled from Pataliputra through provinces, officials and a large army. It is known from the Arthashastra, Megasthenes and Ashoka's edicts.

We run Brahmi workshops, walks to Delhi's Ashokan pillars and study tours to Sanchi for schools, colleges and adult groups.

Mauryan empire: rulers and dates

Chandragupta Maurya took power in Magadha around 321 BCE, traditionally with the help of the Brahmin adviser Chanakya, also called Kautilya. He fought the Greek ruler Seleucus Nicator around 305 BCE; the treaty that followed gave the Mauryas territory in present-day Afghanistan and Baluchistan, and Seleucus sent Megasthenes as envoy to Pataliputra. Jain tradition says Chandragupta ended his life at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.

His son Bindusara extended control into the Deccan. Bindusara's son Ashoka fought the Kalinga war around 261 BCE, after which he turned to dhamma, a moral policy proclaimed in his inscriptions; see our guide to Ashoka and his edicts. After Ashoka the empire weakened, and around 185 BCE the last Maurya, Brihadratha, was killed by his general Pushyamitra Shunga.

Sources for Mauryan history

The Mauryas are better documented than any earlier Indian state. Kautilya's Arthashastra is a treatise on statecraft, but scholars now think it was compiled over several centuries and reached its present form after the Mauryas, so it is used with care. Megasthenes' Indica is lost and survives only in quotations by later Greek and Roman writers such as Strabo and Arrian.

The most direct evidence is Ashoka's own inscriptions on rocks and pillars, written mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script, with Greek and Aramaic in the north-west. Archaeology adds the remains of Pataliputra at Kumhrar and Bulandi Bagh in Patna, punch-marked coins, Northern Black Polished Ware and polished stone sculpture.

Mauryan administration: notes for students

The Mauryan state is often described as highly centralised. Recent historians soften this: the core around Magadha was tightly run, while distant regions were governed more loosely through provincial centres and local elites. With that caution, these are the standard points.

  • King: the centre of power, advised by a council of ministers (mantriparishad).
  • Provinces: governed from centres such as Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, often under princes (kumaras).
  • Officials named in the edicts: mahamattas (senior officers), rajukas (rural administration and justice), yuktas (record-keeping) and pradeshikas (district level).
  • Dhamma-mahamattas: special officers created by Ashoka to spread dhamma and look after welfare.
  • Revenue: a share of the harvest, often given as one sixth in texts, plus taxes on trade and crafts.
  • Departments in the Arthashastra: superintendents (adhyakshas) for mines, forests, weights, ports, trade and more.
  • Army: Megasthenes describes a large standing army with infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants.
  • Pataliputra: Megasthenes describes a city run by boards dealing with crafts, foreigners, trade and records.

Economy, society and Mauryan art

Agriculture in the Ganga plain was the base of the economy, supported by state-run lands and irrigation works. A Junagadh inscription of the 2nd century CE records that the Sudarshana lake in Gujarat was first built under Chandragupta's governor. Trade ran along the routes later called the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha.

Mauryan art is known for its polished sandstone, from quarries near Chunar. The pillar capitals, especially the lion capital from Sarnath, now India's national emblem, show remarkable finish. The Didarganj yakshi, a polished stone figure in the Bihar Museum, is often dated to this period, though some scholars place it later. The Barabar caves in Bihar, cut for the Ajivika sect, have mirror-polished interiors.

Society and religion under the Mauryas

Megasthenes famously divided Indian society into seven groups, including philosophers, farmers, herders, artisans, soldiers, inspectors and councillors. Historians read this as a foreign observer's attempt to describe occupations and the varna order, not as an accurate census. Buddhist, Jain and Ajivika communities were all active, and the Mauryas supported more than one: Chandragupta is linked with Jainism in tradition, Bindusara with the Ajivikas, and Ashoka with Buddhism.

Ashoka's support for the Buddhist sangha, including sending missions to Sri Lanka and elsewhere according to later chronicles, helped Buddhism spread beyond the Ganga plain. At the same time his edicts insist on respect for Brahmins and all sects, which suggests a ruler trying to hold a varied empire together.

Why did the Mauryan empire decline?

Historians have offered many explanations: weak successors after Ashoka, the cost of running a vast army and bureaucracy, the division of the empire among princes, and pressure from Bactrian Greeks in the north-west. An older argument that Ashoka's pacifism or a Brahmin reaction caused the collapse is now generally regarded as too simple.

Where to see the Mauryas

In Delhi you can see an Ashokan rock edict at Srinivaspuri and two Ashokan pillars moved to the city by Firoz Shah Tughlaq, one of them at Firoz Shah Kotla. The National Museum has Mauryan sculpture and coins, and a museum morning with an archaeologist can focus on them. Further afield, our Sanchi and Vidisha immersion covers the Ashokan pillar and stupa at Sanchi. Read our Indian history timeline for what came before and after.

Questions people ask

Who founded the Mauryan empire?

Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan empire around 321 BCE by overthrowing the Nanda dynasty of Magadha. Tradition credits his adviser Chanakya (Kautilya) with planning the rise to power. His capital was Pataliputra, present-day Patna.

What was the capital of the Mauryan empire?

Pataliputra, at the meeting of the Ganga and Son rivers near present-day Patna in Bihar. Megasthenes described its timber palisade, and excavations at Kumhrar and Bulandi Bagh in Patna have found wooden ramparts and a pillared hall.

Is the Arthashastra a reliable source for Mauryan administration?

Partly. The Arthashastra contains early material but most scholars think it was compiled and revised over several centuries, reaching its present form after the Mauryas. It is best read as a guide to ideas of statecraft and checked against Ashoka's edicts and archaeology.

What were provinces of the Mauryan empire?

Ashoka's inscriptions point to provincial centres at Taxila in the north-west, Ujjayini in Malwa, Tosali in Kalinga and Suvarnagiri in the south. These were often governed by princes and were linked to Pataliputra by roads and officials.

When did the Mauryan empire end?

Around 185 BCE, when the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha was assassinated by his commander Pushyamitra, who founded the Shunga dynasty. By then the empire had already lost much of its territory.
